summary: Observation of the landing and then the silent takeoff of a circular craft on a disused railway line: probably a hoax.
description: On Saturday, November 5, 1960, around 8:30 p.m., two people observed green, orange, and red lights that appeared to be coming from a craft moving slowly in the sky. A few days later, on November 13, around 2:45 a.m., one of the witnesses was intrigued by a green light shining into his bedroom. Waking his partner, she confirmed the flashing green, orange, and red lights and then went back to sleep. The witness then went to his doorstep and observed, about 150 meters away, a circular craft several meters in diameter that landed on an abandoned railway track near the house. The craft, silent and resting on a tripod, emitted orange and green lights. The observation lasted about twenty minutes before the craft silently took off and disappeared in a southwest direction, emitting alternating green lights. Intriguingly, the witness reported his observation to a reporter from a regional newspaper. No trace of the sighting was found at the scene during the police investigation. Investigators interviewed several residents, including two SNCF (French National Railway Company) employees on duty that night at the level crossings in the area: these railway workers reported noticing nothing unusual that evening. During the investigation, the credibility of the main witness, well-known to the authorities, was strongly contested by all those questioned and by representatives of the local authorities. No other testimony regarding this sighting corroborated the witness's account. GEIPAN (French National Gendarmerie Intervention Group) classified this case as "B" and likely a hoax.

summary: Observation of the evolution of a light yellow luminous ball in orange weather: probable observation of ball lightning.
description: Recent testimony (February 16, 2015) of an old observation without a specific date (the 1st is given arbitrarily). The witness reports three observations in the same document: we are dealing here with the third observation. In August 1960, shortly before noon, the witness, then 10 years old, was observing the lightning of a violent storm when he saw a very bright, light yellow ball appear above him. It moved slowly along a straight trajectory; it stopped above the roof of a nearby house, returned to its starting point, and disappeared, hidden by the trees. The observation report of this phenomenon was submitted to the Lightning Laboratory, which identified it as a typical case of ball lightning, as the witness had suspected. The ending isn't so strange; ball lightning often follows the updrafts of cumulonimbus clouds, and the description of the general atmosphere is indicative of a thunderstorm accompanied by an arcus cloud (it's almost dark, with very low cloud cover). It's common to see "chimneys" rising towards the anvil, and often the sky and even a few rays of sunlight are visible during the storm. This case is classified as "B": probable observation of ball lightning. The lack of a precise date prevents formal verification of this hypothesis.

Recent testimony (May 14, 2008) of an old observation: around 7:30 a.m. one morning in 1960 (March, April, or May), two schoolchildren observed a luminous phenomenon from the road that intrigued them. After a few minutes, it disappeared over the horizon. No further information was provided by the witnesses. The lack of details and the early date of the observation make any investigation difficult, if not impossible.

summary: Observation in pre-storm weather of the movement of a swollen fire droplet descending from a cloud: probable observation of ball lightning.
description: Recent account of an old observation: the witness describes an observation made around 1960 without further details (the date given here is an arbitrary day and month). In the late afternoon, two people were on the front steps of a house. A storm was threatening, the sky was dark gray. Looking northeast, they saw a "white, bulbous firedrop" descend vertically from the storm clouds. The observation of this "drop," with its pointed upwards, lasted one to three seconds: the phenomenon disappeared behind a curtain of trees. No noise or fire on the ground followed. The case was submitted to a lightning expert. The expert confirmed that this type of observation is not uncommon: it sometimes happens that one or more luminous spheres descend (like the slow fall of a distress flare) from the base of a cumulonimbus cloud during strong pre-storm weather. Generally, the junction of the sphere with the ground or a structure results in an isolated lightning strike, almost always during a dry thunderstorm. This phenomenon is one of the many facets of ball lightning. This case is classified as a "B" probable ball lightning sighting.
